prompt:
<excerpt id="E1">
For me, a belief has an internal item as its content. What I do can reveal that connection, but the connection to the mental representation is what the belief fundamentally is.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E2">
My bus has been arriving early all week, which somehow makes me feel later than when it runs behind. I have started leaving one song sooner.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E3">
My desk lamp started flickering, so I moved everything to the kitchen table. Now I get better light and crumbs inside my keyboard.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E4">
To me, better arguments are a small achievement worth keeping. I just cannot look at the whole philosophical record and call the gains enormous.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E5">
I think believing or wanting something means standing in a certain relation to a representation inside your head. The mental content is there even when nothing obvious shows in your behavior.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E6">
I can want a holiday while sitting perfectly still. I take that wanting to involve an internal representation of the trip, with me relating to it in a particular way.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E7">
I would rather scientists openly weigh the harm of a missed warning. They could reason without that ethical input, but I think choosing to include it makes their work more responsible.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E8">
I think science could keep ethical and political priorities out of its reasoning, but it should not. Decisions about acceptable error deserve a place for human stakes alongside the evidence.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E9">
I reckon philosophy has moved forward a little. We have sharper distinctions and fewer sloppy arguments, but that seems like a few steps rather than a huge historical leap.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E10">
The point for me is what scientists ought to do, not what they are forced to do. Keeping moral considerations outside their reasoning is possible, and I oppose that choice.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E11">
I get something from reading old debates alongside newer ones: a few confusions really do get cleared up. I count that as limited progress, even when the central dispute survives.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E12">
If philosophy had advanced by huge amounts, I would expect beginners to inherit a much bigger pile of settled answers. That is just a hypothetical test, not my assessment of its history.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E13">
I finally beat the boss that kept knocking me off the bridge. The trick was putting the controller down long enough to stop getting annoyed.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E14">
I still see excluding social priorities from scientific inference as an available choice, just a bad one. I want researchers to include those priorities deliberately when judging which risks are acceptable.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E15">
I associate a name with a particular route to its bearer. That route seems part of what the name means, even when somebody else reaches the same individual differently.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E16">
When I discover that the author I read and the neighbor I met are one person, the names gave me different presentations. I think that difference belongs in their meaning.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E17">
I think a name carries a way of thinking about someone, not just the person at the other end. Otherwise learning that two names belong to one person gets weirdly hard to explain.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E18">
I think a person could return to their own past in some possible reality. Our actual physics might forbid the trip, but that would not make it impossible in every conceivable world.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E19">
The engineering objections leave my view untouched. I believe there could be a coherent reality where someone arrives at a date they already lived through.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E20">
I can picture a traveler meeting their younger self without reality falling apart. For me, the strange consequences do not establish that such a world could never exist.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E21">
I watched three episodes while folding laundry and still have a basket left. Apparently matching socks takes more attention than following the plot.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E22">
I think returning to your own past is impossible even in principle. It is not just a problem with building the right machine; no possible world could contain that kind of trip.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E23">
My take is that convictions and wishes fundamentally amount to characteristic tendencies: how somebody responds, reasons, and feels across situations. There is no separate inner token they must connect with.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E24">
The new grocery store has great bread but puts the milk in the most confusing corner. I have accidentally toured the whole building twice.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E25">
Could a name contribute only its referent, with all the different ways of recognizing that person coming from somewhere else? I am asking how that account handles an informative identity sentence.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E26">
I tried making noodles without checking the instructions and ended up with one enormous clump. A little sesame oil helped, but dinner was mostly a rescue operation.
</excerpt>

</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E6">

</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E7">

</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E9">

</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E10">

</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E12">

</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E14">

</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E15">

</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E16">
I do not buy that every fact comes with a deeper reason. I think at least some features of reality just obtain, with nothing available to explain why.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E17">
Is there a definite answer about that intermediate infinity which we simply cannot reach from the usual axioms? I am asking whether independence really leaves room for an underlying truth.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E18">
My favorite part of the cooking show is still the cleanup montage. I wish my kitchen could sort itself out in twelve seconds too.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E19">
I think explanation has to bottom out in some facts that simply have no explanation. Not everything is a mystery awaiting a solution; some things are just brute.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E20">
I bought a bag of apples intending to bake something and have mostly eaten them standing at the counter. That probably tells you how ambitious my weekend actually was.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E21">
The chapter I read argues that a belief can be justified because the process producing it is reliable, even if the believer cannot reflectively check that. I am describing its position here, not adopting it.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E22">
The train ride was quiet enough that I finished two chapters. Then I missed my stop and got an unplanned walk out of it.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E23">
My headphones survived another trip through the bottom of my backpack. The case looks terrible, but the left side has finally stopped making that clicking noise.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E24">
I am less confident that explanation really has to hit a brute stopping point. The demand for a reason behind everything is pulling at me, though I am not ready to endorse it.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E25">
I tried the soup place near the station. The bowl was enormous, and I carried the leftovers home like they were something fragile.
</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E26">
I finally hung the print that had been leaning against my bookshelf for months. Finding the hooks took longer than choosing a spot, and I managed to drop one behind the radiator. I think artistic merit depends on how people experience a work. The room looks more finished now, though the empty packaging is still sitting beside the door waiting for me to take it out.
</excerpt>

</excerpt>
<excerpt id="E26">
